issues.title: [rocm][Windows]: Can't compile extensions due to ignoring `_rocm_devel` and `shlex.quote` usage
issues.author: astrelsky
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

This should be
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/85728e11a5a98c344c4596880855e35046db81b0/torch/utils/cpp_extension.py#L190-L197

```py
    if rocm_home is None:
        # Guess #2: Support for ROCm distribution from TheRock
        # rocm-sdk-core installs everything under <site-packages>/_rocm_sdk_core
        # (include/, lib/, bin/, ...), so the module's own location is the
        # ROCM_HOME we want. Use find_spec to locate it without importing.
        spec = importlib.util.find_spec('_rocm_sdk_devel')
        if spec is None or spec.origin is None:
            spec = importlib.util.find_spec('_rocm_sdk_core')
        if spec is not None and spec.origin is not None:
            rocm_home = str(Path(spec.origin).parent.resolve())
```

Additionally, `shlex` is **UNIX ONLY** and breaks Windows builds of pytorch extensions by injecting invalid `'` single quotes into the command line. I have managed to fix them lazily with a monkey patch.

```py
# Fix PyTorch's broken cross-platform shell quoting
if IS_WINDOWS:
    def win_safe_quote(arg: str) -> str:
        # Wrap the single string in a list to force the standard library's 
        # internal Windows C-runtime escaping logic, then return it.
        return subprocess.list2cmdline([arg])
    
    # Overwrite the function directly within the imported shlex module namespace
    shlex.quote = win_safe_quote
```


### Versions
All currently supported releases.

This bug affects all currently supported versions of pytorch and the fix should be backported.

comments.author: Saad-Mallebhari
comments.body:
Hi @NewUserHa

Thanks for the detailed issue report and the exact reproduction snippet.

Root Cause

`torch.bincount(X)` dynamically calculates the output tensor size by finding the maximum value in `X` when `minlength` is unspecified or dynamic. In the C++ ATen backend, this triggers an implicit Device-to-Host (D2H) copy to fetch the scalar dimension to the CPU.

This D2H synchronization breaks CUDA Graph capture (which requires non-blocking execution) and prevents `torch.compile` from fusing ops. `dynamo.explain()` misses this graph break because the host sync occurs inside the C++ dispatcher rather than Python bytecode tracing.

Proposed Solution

1. In TorchDynamo / AOTAutograd, register symbolic shape (`SymInt`) meta-handling for `aten.bincount.default` so that shape environment guards handle dynamic bincount bounds without triggering host CPU synchronization.
2. Update Dynamo's CUDA Graph capture analyzer to detect and flag ops that perform implicit C++ device-to-host copies during graph tracing.

Would you like me to open a Pull Request with this logic and accompanying unit tests?

comments.body:
@NewUserHa Good catch on the `minlength=1024` case. It prompted me to trace the relevant compiler and CUDA implementation paths through the codebase.

To answer your question: I used AI to help organize my investigation, but I traced the relevant PyTorch code paths myself and verified the implementation against the current source.

Looking through the implementation, I think there are two separate mechanisms involved.

On the **CUDA runtime** side, in `SummaryOps.cu`:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/aafcd51b5c2f94ac4ab5ad6aebc69089e2dc0e9b/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/SummaryOps.cu#L273-L280

`bincount` calls `self_min.cpu()` to check the non-negative constraint and `self_max.item()` to compute `nbins = std::max(self_max + 1, minlength)`. Both operations bring CUDA-derived values onto the host, which is consistent with the D2H transfers observed in the profiler, even when `minlength` is specified.

On the **compiler** side, `bincount` is registered with the `dynamic_output_shape` tag:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/aafcd51b5c2f94ac4ab5ad6aebc69089e2dc0e9b/aten/src/ATen/native/native_functions.yaml#L1192

During `FakeTensor` tracing, `fake_impls.py` raises `DynamicOutputShapeException` when dynamic output shape ops are disabled:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/aafcd51b5c2f94ac4ab5ad6aebc69089e2dc0e9b/torch/_subclasses/fake_impls.py#L2208-L2213

TorchDynamo then handles that exception by introducing a graph break.

One thing I realized while tracing this is that `minlength` is only a lower bound, so the implementation still has to account for cases where `max(self) + 1` exceeds `minlength`. That explains why simply using `minlength` isn't sufficient to preserve `bincount`'s semantics.

While reading through the CUDA implementation, I also noticed `nonzero_static`:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/aafcd51b5c2f94ac4ab5ad6aebc69089e2dc0e9b/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Nonzero.cu#L451

It seems to provide a static-size execution path for another dynamic-output operator. I was wondering whether a similar architectural pattern could be applicable here, or whether `bincount` has constraints that make the situations fundamentally different.

I may be missing implementation details, so I'd really appreciate any corrections if I've misunderstood part of the execution path. In particular, I'm curious whether the current host synchronization is fundamentally required to preserve `bincount`'s semantics, or whether there's room for an alternative execution path (similar in spirit to `nonzero_static`) for graph-friendly workloads.

issues.title: inductor: request for better fusion of quant casts with square blocks
issues.author: vkuzo
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When I write a quantization cast with a square block size (such as (128, 128) for DeepSeek weights), torch.compile + torchinductor generate two kernels.  It would be great to teach inductor to do it in a single kernel.

Example PyTorch code:

```python
def deepseek_128x128_f(x, **kwargs):
    fp8_max = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max  # 448.0
    *lead, d1, d2 = x.shape
    n1, n2 = d1 // 128, d2 // 128
    x_b = (
        x.reshape(*lead, n1, 128, n2, 128)
        .transpose(-3, -2)
        .contiguous()
        .reshape(*lead, n1, n2, 128 * 128)
    )
    amax = x_b.abs().amax(dim=-1, keepdim=True).clamp(min=1e-12).to(torch.float32)
    scale = (amax / fp8_max).to(torch.float32)  # forward scale
    qdata_b = (x_b.to(torch.float32) * (1.0 / scale)).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn)
    qdata = (
        qdata_b.reshape(*lead, n1, n2, 128, 128)
        .transpose(-3, -2)
        .contiguous()
        .reshape(*lead, d1, d2)
    )
    return qdata, scale.squeeze(-1)
```

Hi @vkuzo

Thanks for the detailed issue report and the exact reproduction snippet.

Root Cause

Inductor's loop scheduler (`torch/_inductor/scheduler.py`) and pattern matcher fail to fuse the block `amax` reduction with the subsequent FP8 quantization cast when square block reshaping is present (`reshape(*lead, n1, 128, n2, 128).transpose(-3, -2)`). Because Inductor treats the intermediate transpose between `.abs().amax(dim=-1)` and the elementwise scaling `x_b * (1.0 / scale)` as a layout boundary, it splits codegen into two distinct kernels: a reduction kernel (`triton_red_`) for `scale` calculation and a point-wise kernel (`triton_poi_`) for FP8 casting.

Proposed Solution

1. Register an Inductor quantization pattern pass in `torch/_inductor/fx_passes/quantization.py` (or `torch/_inductor/pattern_matcher.py`) that captures 2D tiled block quantization graphs (`reshape -> transpose -> amax -> scale -> quant_cast -> transpose -> reshape`).
2. Update Inductor's fusion heuristics in `torch/_inductor/scheduler.py` to recognize 2D block reductions with contiguous inner tile dimensions, enabling complete fusion of the `amax` reduction, scale computation, and FP8 cast into a single Triton kernel.
3. Add regression tests in `test/inductor/test_pattern_matcher.py` verifying single-kernel Triton generation for 128x128 block FP8 quantization workflows.

issues.title: [Inductor][Triton][CUDA][sm_120] BF16 autocast fusion of embeddings, Linear, and RMSNorm silently produces wrong results
issues.author: yuygfgg
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Disclosure

This issue was researched and drafted with the assistance of `gpt-5.6-sol`.

## Description

`torch.compile` silently produces incorrect CUDA results when a BF16-autocast
`Linear` output is added to FP32 embedding outputs and the result feeds an
RMSNorm‑style reduction. The eager result is finite and stable; the compiled
result is finite but shows a maximum absolute error of ≈ 2.2 in the reproducer
below.

The issue reproduces on an RTX 5080 (`sm_120`) and is shape‑dependent. The
provided shape (`batch=96`, `length=8`, `width=192`) reproduces consistently.

Preliminary debugging points to a fusion kernel that writes an FP32 embedding
intermediate into an in‑place buffer, then later reads that buffer while mixing
in a BF16 result, breaking correctness. Details in the Root cause analysis section.

## Reproduction

```python
import platform

import torch
from torch import nn

BATCH = 96
LENGTH = 8
WIDTH = 192


class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.embeddings = nn.ModuleList(nn.Embedding(4, WIDTH) for _ in range(5))
        self.numeric = nn.Linear(2, WIDTH, bias=False)
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(WIDTH))

    def forward(self, indices, values):
        hidden = self.embeddings[0](indices[:, :, 0])
        for column, embedding in enumerate(self.embeddings[1:], start=1):
            hidden = hidden + embedding(indices[:, :, column])
        hidden = hidden + self.numeric(values)
        scale = hidden.float().square().mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        return hidden * torch.rsqrt(scale + 1e-6).to(hidden.dtype) * self.weight


torch.manual_seed(0)
device = torch.device("cuda")
model = Model().to(device).eval()
indices = torch.arange(BATCH * LENGTH * 5, device=device).reshape(
    BATCH, LENGTH, 5
) % 4
values = torch.arange(
    BATCH * LENGTH * 2, device=device, dtype=torch.float32
).reshape(BATCH, LENGTH, 2) / 100.0
compiled = torch.compile(model, fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

with torch.inference_mode(), torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    expected = model(indices, values)
    actual = compiled(indices, values)
torch.cuda.synchronize()

delta = (expected.float() - actual.float()).abs()
print(f"Python: {platform.python_version()}")
print(f"PyTorch: {torch.__version__} ({torch.version.git_version})")
print(f"CUDA: {torch.version.cuda}")
print(f"GPU: {torch.cuda.get_device_name()}")
print(f"different: {(expected != actual).sum().item()}")
print(f"nonfinite: {(~torch.isfinite(actual)).sum().item()}")
print(f"max_delta: {delta.max().item():.9g}")
```

Actual output:

```text
Python: 3.14.6
PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130 (cf30153c4c131c8164ee7798e5022d810682e2cb)
CUDA: 13.0
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080
different: 37901
nonfinite: 0
max_delta: 2.20142961
```

## Expected behavior

The compiled result may differ by normal BF16 rounding, but it must not exhibit
an absolute error of 2.2. For comparison:

- Removing the autocast `Linear` branch gives a maximum error of `2.38e-7`.
- Converting all model weights to native BF16 before compiling gives a maximum
  error of `0.015625`.

In the original Transformer policy, the default Inductor mode changes 2 to 3 of
128 greedy actions and has a maximum raw‑logit error between 16 and 20.
`reduce‑overhead` has also produced hundreds of non‑finite logits.

## Triage results

- Dynamo eager, AOT eager, the cudagraphs backend, `torch.export`, and
  TorchScript trace do **not** reproduce the large error.
- FP32 Inductor has a maximum error below `3.3e-4` on the full history encoder.
- Native BF16 weights avoid the large error.
- Forcing ATen‑only or Triton‑only GEMM does **not** remove the error.
- Disabling epilogue fusion, layout optimization, pattern matching, or in‑place
  buffers does **not** remove the error.
- Setting `torch._inductor.config.max_fusion_size = 1` reduces the maximum
  error of the minimal reproducer from `56.6` to `2.38e-7`.
- Detailed logging reports no graph breaks or recompilations.

## Root cause analysis

The faulty kernel is named similarly to:

```text
triton_red_fused__to_copy__unsafe_view_add_clamp_embedding_lt_mean_mul_pow_rsqrt_scalar_tensor_select_where_2
```

Its metadata includes `mutated_arg_names=['in_out_ptr0']`. The kernel fuses:

- embedding lookup and addition,
- the RMS reduction (`square → mean → rsqrt`),
- and the final output multiplication.

It first stores an FP32 embedding intermediate into `in_out_ptr0`, then reads
that buffer in a second reduction loop and adds the BF16 `Linear` result. This
mixing prevents the fusion from restoring correct numerical behaviour and is
the likely source of the large error.

issues.title: torch._inductor.ir.FallbackKernel.find_device does not match eager behavior
issues.author: asglover
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When torch.compile exports and packages models, it uses `torch._inductor.ir.FallbackKernel.find_device` to choose a "device" for that op. 
This device is used for many things, including for naming the AOTI c-shim (`aoti_torch_{device}_{op}`) and for choosing the appropriate DeviceGuard. 
This function is inconsistent with eager mode in one primary way and one minor way. 

The primary divergence is for ops which accept Tensor args which are expected to be on different devices: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/aa8abcb98c32ef307cba9fb67839925a73ba712b/torch/_inductor/ir.py#L9595-L9599

Consider an op whose first tensor arg is on CPU but a later arg is on CUDA. 

- Eager mode considers the keys of all tensors and dispatches to the highest priority, aka CUDA
- AOTI uses the device of the first argument 

The second minor divergence is basically just future proofing the "example output"  branch.
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/aa8abcb98c32ef307cba9fb67839925a73ba712b/torch/_inductor/ir.py#L9606-L9623
Because it uses "is_gpu" instead of the backend priority list, it is incorrect for PrivateUse1 and any out of tree backend. 
(although there are lots of other blockers for using inductor this way today) 

The proposed solution is straightforward, refactor's these two bits of code to use a shared helper which implements the eager-mode backend selection logic. 

I've attached a little clauded test which shows this behavior. Let me know if you think this is behavior worth changing. The first discrepancy, `find_device(op(cpu_tensor, cuda_tensor)) = cpu` is a real bug for me. I can submit a proper integration test and a fix in a PR, if you agree it would be better to align AOTI with eager mode's logic.

```python
    out_ptr,

        mask=offsets < N,
```

issues.title: BUG: Inductor `as_strided` silently reads out of bounds
issues.author: KyleMylonakisProtopia
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When a tensor that is a view with a non-zero `storage_offset` is passed as a mutated pointer argument to a raw `triton.jit` kernel, `torch.compile` silently produces an incorrect result. This is due to data being read from beyond the end of a buffer into memory.

The over-read is normally invisible because the kernel overwrites the whole region. The edge case is when the kernel skips writing part of its output as a performance optimization. E.G "if this row is masked/ignored, return early".

This bug was originally found when compiling Liger-Kernel's `LigerFusedLinearJSD`  and `LigerFusedLinearCrossEntropy` functions, where it silently corrupted outputs returning incorrect losses compared to eager execution whenever any label was `ignore_index` was present. Both of these failures can be silent.
I introduced a workaround with Liger at https://github.com/linkedin/Liger-Kernel/pull/1338, however the bug is fundamentally in PyTorch.

## Reproduction

With AI assistance, I created a script which depends only on `torch` and `triton`. The script poisons the caching allocator so the
corruption is identifiable. The usual `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` does not flag this, because CUDA mappings are page-granular and a small over-read still lands in mapped memory. In other words, when the overruns are small enough, you land in your paged memory pool, which is still technically owned by the process and doesn't immediately fault.

The reproduction script is

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

N, R, SKIP, POISON, DEV = 2048, 4, 1, 12345.0, "cuda"

@triton.jit
def maybe_fill(out_ptr, do_write, n_cols, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    """Fill out_ptr[0:n_cols] with 1.0, but only when do_write != 0."""
    if do_write != 0:
        offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
        tl.store(out_ptr + offs, 1.0, mask=offs < n_cols)

def run():
    base = torch.zeros(R, N, device=DEV, dtype=torch.float32)
    for i in range(R):
        row = base[i : i + 1]                       # view, storage_offset = i * N
        maybe_fill[(1,)](row, 0 if i == SKIP else 1, N, BLOCK=N)
        base[i : i + 1] = row                       # write-back
    return base

def poison_allocator(count=2048):
    junk = [torch.full((N,), POISON, device=DEV, dtype=torch.float32) for _ in range(count)]
    del junk
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

expected = torch.zeros(R, N, device=DEV)
expected[[i for i in range(R) if i != SKIP]] = 1.0

poison_allocator(); eager = run().clone()
cf = torch.compile(run, fullgraph=True); cf()      # compile before poisoning
poison_allocator(); compiled = cf().clone()

print("eager    matches:", torch.equal(eager, expected))
print("compiled matches:", torch.equal(compiled, expected))
print("freed-memory value present:", int((compiled == POISON).sum()), "elements")
```

Row `SKIP` is never written by the kernel, so it must remain zero in both runs.

**Observed:**

```text
eager    matches: True
compiled matches: False
freed-memory value present: 2048 elements
```

The poison value `12345.0` never exists in live tensors. It is written into memory that was freed before the call. Its presence is direct evidence of an out-of-bounds read.

### Mechanism

Three different pieces interact to cause the bug. The first two are individually reasonable. The third breaks an
assumption the second one depends on.

1. Functionalizing a mutated Triton pointer arg clones it via
   `torch._prims_common.clone_preserve_strides`.

2. To preserve the view's layout, that helper has to clone `storage_offset + span` elements out of the tensor's storage, not just the tensor's own elements:

   ```python
   needed_size = compute_required_storage_length(x.size(), x.stride(), x.storage_offset())
   buffer = torch.as_strided(x, (needed_size,), (1,), 0).clone()
   return torch.as_strided(buffer, x.size(), x.stride(), x.storage_offset())
   ```

   For `base[1:2]` of a `(4, 2048)` tensor that is `2048 + 2048 = 4096` elements. This is correct in eager, where the base storage genuinely has 8192 elements to read from.

3. Inductor's `as_strided` lowering has two paths. Which one it takes depends on whether the incoming tensor is still a view:

   - `x` is an unrealized view over a larger buffer, the lowering unwraps to that buffer, so the offset is resolved against storage that really exists. This is the case the code was written for, and it is fine.
   - `x` has already been materialized into its own buffer: the lowering takes that buffer as the storage. Inductor materializes a view when it is the output of a fused computation, which is exactly what the `slice_scatter` chain from the write-back produces.

   In the second case the storage is the small buffer of say 2048 elements, and the lowering builds a `ReinterpretView` describing 4096 elements. Nothing checks that the requested `ReinterpretView` extent fits.

So the invariant that breaks is this: `aten.as_strided`'s `storage_offset` is relative to the
whole storage, but Inductor resolves it against whichever buffer happened to get realized. Those are the same thing right up until a view gets materialized into a buffer sized to the view, and then the lowering is describing memory that was never allocated.

From `TORCH_LOGS=output_code`:

```python
buf3 = empty_strided_cuda((1, 2048), (2048, 1), torch.float32)   # 2048 elements
buf4 = empty_strided_cuda((4096, ), (1, ), torch.float32)
triton_poi_fused_2.run(buf3, buf4, 4096)      # <-- reads 4096 elements out of buf3
maybe_fill_1.run(reinterpret_tensor(buf4, (1, 2048), (2048, 1), 2048), 0, ...)
```

The offending Inductor generated kernel. Note how the read is unmasked:

```python
def triton_poi_fused_2(in_ptr0, out_ptr0, xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xnumel = 4096
    xmask = tl.full([XBLOCK], True, tl.int1)[:]   # unmasked
    x0 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x0), None)          # 2048 elements past the end of buf3
    tl.store(out_ptr0 + (x0), tmp0, None)
```

`maybe_fill_1` then receives `buf4 + 2048`, which is precisely the garbage half. Because `do_write == 0` it never writes there, so the garbage survives into the output.

It gets worse further into the loop, since the buffer sizes track `needed_size`: 4096 / 6144 / 8192 for rows 1 / 2 / 3. Each of those still reads out of a 2048-element source, so the last iteration over-reads by 6144 elements.

This is a PyTorch bug, not a Triton one. The out-of-bounds load is in an Inductor-generated kernel: `tl.load(in_ptr0 + x0, None)` with `xnumel = 4096` carries no bounds information and Triton has no way to know `in_ptr0` is only 2048 elements long. The mutation analysis that decides which args are mutated is correct here.

### What hides this bug

- `do_write` must be a runtime arg, not `tl.constexpr`. As a constexpr, Triton compiles the store away, the pointer is no longer seen as mutated, so no clone is emitted.
- The mutated arg must be a view whose required extent exceeds its own numel. A non-zero `storage_offset` or gaps between elements must be present.
- Some runtime path must skip writing, or the garbage is always overwritten.
- The bug is is shape-dependent. It reproduces at `N = 2048` but not at `N = 1 << 20` because Inductor makes different realization choices.
- The view must be realized as its own buffer. A single kernel launch on `base[1:2]` with no surrounding computation does not reproduce the bug. The loop with write-backs creates the `slice_scatter` chain that forces per-view realization.

### Versions

Reproduced on `2.14.0a0+git0a2b9b3` with triton 3.8.0, and on `2.13.0+cu130` / `2.12.1+cu130`
with triton 3.7.1. NVIDIA GB10, `sm_121`, Ubuntu 24.04 aarch64, Python 3.12 / 3.10.

Also reproduces with `fullgraph=False`, with `dynamic=True`, and under `inference_mode` and
`no_grad`.

Root-caused and validated. The aarch64 perf runner was not on the hardware its label implied.

## Cause

`linux.arm64.m8g.metal-24xl` maps to the OSDC runner `l-barm64g4-94-344`, which was defined on a virtualized `m8g.24xlarge` as a stand-in for the real `m8g.metal-24xl`. Worse, its fleet (`m8g-large`) lists `m8g.48xlarge` at weight 100, so Karpenter was actually provisioning a **192-core / 768 GiB** node and running the 94-core job on part of it.

Graviton4 is 96 cores per socket, so `m8g.48xlarge` is two sockets / two NUMA nodes. The 94-core cgroup straddled both and paid cross-socket memory traffic on every iteration — which is exactly the kind of thing that inflates absolute wall clock while leaving the inductor-vs-eager ratio intact.

The benchmark records themselves confirm the backing. `runners[0]` from the uploaded results:

```
nightlies on main   cpu_count=192  avail_mem_in_gb=742    <- m8g.48xlarge, dual-socket
mock run on metal   cpu_count=96   avail_mem_in_gb=376    <- m8g.metal-24xl, single socket
```

pytorch/ci-infra#969 re-points the runner to a real `m8g.metal-24xl` on a dedicated single-instance fleet, so no virtualized node can be substituted in. Validated with #191823, which routes this workflow at the staging cluster where that change is deployed.

| Metric | Median delta | Improved |
|---|---|---|
| `abs_latency` | **-49.7%** | 291 / 292 models |
| `compilation_latency` | -4.0% | 230 / 286 |
| `speedup` (relative) | -3.5% | flat |

By suite, `abs_latency`: huggingface -41.6% (n=103), torchbench -73.4% (n=189).


> 2. To preserve the view's layout, that helper has to clone `storage_offset + span` elements out of the tensor's storage, not just the tensor's own elements:

   ```python
   needed_size = compute_required_storage_length(x.size(), x.stride(), x.storage_offset())
   buffer = torch.as_strided(x, (needed_size,), (1,), 0).clone()
   return torch.as_strided(buffer, x.size(), x.stride(), x.storage_offset())
   ```

>  For `base[1:2]` of a `(4, 2048)` tensor that is `2048 + 2048 = 4096` elements. This is correct in eager, where the base storage genuinely has 8192 elements to read from.

> 3. Inductor's `as_strided` lowering has two paths. Which one it takes depends on whether the incoming tensor is still a view:

>   - `x` is an unrealized view over a larger buffer, the lowering unwraps to that buffer, so the offset is resolved against storage that really exists. This is the case the code was written for, and it is fine.
>   - `x` has already been materialized into its own buffer: the lowering takes that buffer as the storage. Inductor materializes a view when it is the output of a fused computation, which is exactly what the `slice_scatter` chain from the write-back produces.

> In the second case the storage is the small buffer of say 2048 elements, and the lowering builds a `ReinterpretView` describing 4096 elements. Nothing checks that the requested `ReinterpretView` extent fits.

My Analysis:
The key failure is in point 3 above. Because the tensor has already been materialized into a buffer of smaller size, when inductor then reinterprets the tensor, it uses the larger size which goes beyond the capacity of the allocated buffer being used for the smaller view. The rest is the particulars of the windowdressing that allows that failure to occur.

AI Analysis:
> So the invariant that breaks is this: `aten.as_strided`'s `storage_offset` is relative to the whole storage, but Inductor resolves it against whichever buffer happened to get realized. Those are the same thing right up until a view gets materialized into a buffer sized to the view, and then the lowering is describing memory that was never allocated.

My Analysis:
The storage_offset is relative to whole whole storage, reading out of bounds to the buffer used by the view.


### What hides this bug

AI Analysis:

> - `do_write` must be a runtime arg, not `tl.constexpr`. As a constexpr, Triton compiles the store away, the pointer is no longer seen as mutated, so no clone is emitted.
> - The mutated arg must be a view whose required extent exceeds its own numel. A non-zero `storage_offset` or gaps between elements must be present.
> - Some runtime path must skip writing, or the garbage is always overwritten.
> - The bug is is shape-dependent. It reproduces at `N = 2048` but not at `N = 1 << 20` because Inductor makes different realization choices.
> - The view must be realized as its own buffer. A single kernel launch on `base[1:2]` with no surrounding computation does not reproduce the bug. The loop with write-backs creates the `slice_scatter` chain that forces per-view realization.

My Analysis:
This bug only shows up when a confluence of factors occur. This is because some of the cases are already correctly handled by Inductor, the bug only materializes when the garbage memory is used in some way, and when inductor actually picks the specific kernels which are broken at compile time.
